issues.legal_issue: A factual finding made by the first appellate court cannot be set aside in a second appeal merely by re-evaluating the facts.
material_facts: The first appellate court examined the evidence and found that the entries recording the respondents as occupants were fictitious and had been made fraudulently.
The High Court proceeded on the mistaken assumption that the first appellate court had made no finding on fraud and relied on the entries to reverse its decree.
issues.conclusion: The High Court had no jurisdiction in the second appeal to set aside the first appellate court’s factual finding that the entries were fraudulent; its judgment was set aside and the first appellate court’s decree restored.
issues.legal_principle: Under sections 100–103 of the Code of Civil Procedure, a second appeal does not permit the High Court to set aside a factual finding made by the first appellate court on whether entries were genuine or fraudulent. The Court held that this was a question of fact.

predicates.second_appeal: The proceeding is a second appeal from a decree of a subordinate court.
predicates.first_appellate_court_made_factual_findi: The first appellate court examined the evidence and made a finding on a factual issue.
predicates.factual_finding_cannot_be_set_aside_in_s: A factual finding made by the first appellate court cannot be set aside in the second appeal.

issues.definition: When a second appeal challenges a factual finding made by the first appellate court, that finding cannot be set aside in the second appeal.

issues.legal_issue: A High Court determining a factual issue for itself in a second appeal must discuss the evidence on that issue.
material_facts: The High Court assumed that the first appellate court had not made a clear finding on whether the revenue entries were fraudulent.
The High Court did not discuss the evidence and instead relied on the entries to reverse the first appellate court’s decision.
issues.conclusion: Even if the High Court had to determine the issue of fraud for itself, it could not do so without discussing the evidence; its reliance on the entries without such discussion was erroneous.
issues.legal_principle: Section 103 of the Code of Civil Procedure permits the High Court in a second appeal to determine an issue of fact in the circumstances specified by that section, but when it does so it must discuss the evidence relevant to that issue.

predicates.second_appeal: The proceeding is a second appeal from a decree of a subordinate court.
predicates.high_court_determines_factual_issue: The High Court determines a factual issue for itself in the second appeal.
predicates.evidence_not_discussed: The High Court does not discuss the evidence relevant to the factual issue.
predicates.factual_determination_is_erroneous: The High Court’s determination of the factual issue is erroneous.

issues.definition: If the High Court determines a factual issue in a second appeal without discussing the relevant evidence, its determination is erroneous.

issues.legal_issue: A fraudulent or forged revenue entry does not receive the presumption of correctness and cannot support a claim to possessory title based on that entry.
material_facts: The respondents relied on revenue entries recording them as occupants to claim a right to retain the lands.
The first appellate court considered the evidence and found that the entries had been made fictitiously, surreptitiously and fraudulently.
The claim to protection as occupants depended on the entries rather than proof of actual possession.
issues.conclusion: The presumption of correctness did not apply to the fraudulent entries, and they could not support the respondents’ claim to possessory title.
issues.legal_principle: Under section 20(b)(ii) of the U.P. Zamindari Abolition and Land Reforms Act, 1951, the relevant record entry is ordinarily accepted without an inquiry into actual possession. Amba Prasad v. Abdul Noor Khan and Sonawati v. Sri Ram explain the role of such entries in an adhivasi claim. The presumption of correctness applies to genuine entries, but proof of fraud displaces it; fraud or forgery robs a document of legal effect and it cannot found possessory title.

predicates.entry_is_fraudulent: The entry was made fictitiously, surreptitiously or fraudulently.
predicates.entry_cannot_support_possessory_title: The entry cannot support a claim to possessory title.
predicates.claim_based_on_revenue_entry and entry_i: A person claims a right to retain land on the basis of an entry recording that person as an occupant, and the entry was made fictitiously, surreptitiously or fraudulently.

issues.definition: When a claim to retain land rests on a revenue entry that is fraudulent, the entry cannot support possessory title.
